summary: Jesus tells of a steward, about to lose his post, who wins friends by reducing his master’s debtors’ bills, and teaches His disciples faithfulness with money.
key_insight: In the same sentence the steward is praised by his master and called “unjust.” The praise is not for what the man did but for how he thought: he saw the end coming and used what was still in his hands to prepare for it. “The sons of this world are more shrewd in their generation than the sons of light.”
story: Jesus also said to His disciples, “There was a certain rich man who had a steward, and an accusation was brought to him that this man was wasting his goods.” The rich man called him in: “What is this I hear about you? Give an account of your stewardship, for you can no longer be steward.”

The steward said to himself, “What shall I do? For my master is taking the stewardship away from me. I cannot dig; I am ashamed to beg.” Then he made up his mind. He would act now, so that when he was put out of his post, people would welcome him into their homes.

He called in his master’s debtors one by one. He asked the first, “How much do you owe my master?” The man said, “A hundred measures of oil.” The steward told him, “Take your bill, and sit down quickly and write fifty.” To another, who owed a hundred measures of wheat, he said, “Take your bill, and write eighty.”
“So the master commended the unjust steward because he had dealt shrewdly,” Jesus said. “For the sons of this world are more shrewd in their generation than the sons of light.”

“And I say to you, make friends for yourselves by unrighteous mammon, that when you fail, they may receive you into an everlasting home.” Whoever is faithful in very little is faithful also in much, and whoever is unjust in little is unjust in much. If they had not been faithful with unrighteous mammon, who would trust them with the true riches? If they had not been faithful with what belonged to another, who would give them what was their own?
“No servant can serve two masters; for either he will hate the one and love the other, or else he will be loyal to the one and despise the other. You cannot serve God and mammon.”

scene.label: A steward
scene.text: A steward managed a rich man’s estate. He collected rents, made loans and kept the accounts, and he could act in his master’s name. This one was probably a free man rather than a slave: once dismissed, he faced either hard labor or begging.

scene.label: Oil and wheat
scene.text: The oil was measured in baths, each several gallons; the wheat in kors, a far larger measure. A hundred of either was a large commercial debt, probably owed by tenant farmers paying rent in produce or by merchants buying on credit. The steward had each debtor change the bill in his own hand.

scene.label: What did he cut?
scene.text: Views differ. Many hold that he simply cheated his master again, lowering the debts so the debtors would owe him a favor. Others think the bills included his own commission, or interest the Law forbade charging a fellow Israelite (Deuteronomy 23:19), so he gave up what was not rightly owed and left his master looking generous. Either way, the praise is only for his shrewdness, and Jesus still calls him “the unjust steward.”

scene.label: Which master?
scene.text: The NKJV reads “the master commended” (v. 8). The Greek word can also mean “the lord,” and a few take it to mean Jesus. Most read it as the rich man in the story, since Jesus’ own comment begins in the next verse: “And I say to you” (v. 9).

scene.label: An everlasting home
scene.text: Jesus’ phrase is literally eternal tents or dwellings. Money cannot go with anyone into eternity, but money given away now can make friends who will be there to welcome the giver.

witnesses.luke: Only Luke records this parable. He sets it right after the prodigal son, who also “wasted” what he had been given (15:13; 16:1), and right before the Pharisees, “lovers of money,” sneer at it (16:14). No Gospel says more about money than Luke, and here Jesus teaches that wealth, which cannot last, can still be used for what will.

seeing.reveals: Jesus speaks plainly about money because He knows it competes for the heart: “You cannot serve God and mammon.” He can find a lesson even in an unjust man’s cleverness, a lesson His own followers are slow to learn.
seeing.living: Every steward will give an account, and nothing we hold now goes with us. Use money while it is in your hands to bless people, especially those in need, in ways that will matter in eternity. Faithfulness with little is where God trains us for the true riches.
seeing.ponder: If you knew your stewardship ended soon, what would you do differently with the money in your hands today?

preaching.big_idea: Be as wise for eternity as the world is for tomorrow; money tests whom you serve.
outline: Faithful in little, loyal to one Master (10–13)
preaching.watch_for: This parable is not an allegory in which every figure stands for someone. It makes one point, stated in verse 8, and Jesus then applies it three ways (vv. 9, 10–12, 13). Do not look for God in the rich man or try to excuse the steward.

title: The Shrewd Steward
